subjectPhysics
chapterUnits and Measurements high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on expressing a distance in a new system of units where c = 1, so distance = c x t = 400 new units, which is conversion of units / choice of system of units.
subtopic 1System of Units
why this subtopicThe answer depends on reading the new system of units in which c = 1, so the unit of length is the distance light covers in 1 s and the Sun-Earth distance is just the travel time 400 s expressed as 400 new units.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
The speed of light in vacuum is taken as unity. If light takes 6 min 40 s to reach the Earth from the Sun, the distance between the Sun and the Earth in new unit is:
  1. 3 × 108
  2. 500
  3. 3 × 1010
  4. 400
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
  1. Time, t = 6 min 40 s
  2. = 360 + 40
  3. = 400 s
  4. Distance in new system d = vt
  5. = 1 × 400 = 400

→ the working concludes: option 4

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. Convert the travel time: t = 6 min 40 s = 6 × 60 + 40 = 400 s.
  2. In the new system the speed of light is unity, so c = 1 distance-unit per second.
  3. d = c t = 1 × 400 = 400 new units, which is option 4.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
44 highagree
difficultymedium · 2 steps
stepsChange 6 min 40 s into seconds. It is 400 s. → In this new system c = 1. Distance = c x t. So the distance in new units is the same number as the time in seconds.
confusing options2 of 4 · options 4, 2
400 is what the time printed in this question gives you. 500 is the number you have memorised for sunlight reaching Earth, because that trip takes 8 min 20 s, which is 500 s. So 500 is where you land if you answer from memory instead of reading the 6 min 40 s given here.
why it is trickyThere is only one step. But the paper changed a number you already know. Sunlight takes 8 min 20 s, which is 500 s. Here the question says 6 min 40 s, which is 400 s. If you answer from memory you pick 500. If you read the question you pick 400. The other two numbers, 3 x 108 and 3 x 1010, are just speed-of-light values. Once c = 1, no working leads to them.
the catchThis is a memory trap, not a maths mistake. You have to notice that the question changed the usual number. You also have to see that c = 1 makes the answer the same number as the time in seconds.

Q2Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterMechanical Properties of Solids high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on the defining formulae of Young's modulus, bulk modulus, compressibility and Poisson's ratio, the elastic moduli taught in mechanical properties of solids.
subtopic 1Hooke's Law
why this subtopicThe answer depends on the defining formulae of the elastic moduli - Young's modulus FL/A(dL), compressibility, bulk modulus and Poisson's ratio - which are the elastic constants introduced with Hooke's law.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
Match List I with List II:

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
A.Young's ModulusI.Δ dΔ L(Ld)
B.CompressibilityII.FLA(Δ L)
C.Bulk ModulusIII.-1Δ P(Δ VV)
D.Poisson's RatioIV.-P(VΔ V)
  1. A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III
  2. A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV
  3. A-I, B-IV, C-III, D-II
  4. A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
  1. A. Young's Modulus = StressStrain = FLAΔ L
  2. B. Compressibility = 1Bulk modulus = -1Δ P(Δ VV)
  3. C. Bulk Modulus = -P(VΔ V)
  4. D. Poisson's Ratio = Lateral strainLongitudinal strain = Δ dΔ L(Ld)

→ the working concludes: option 4

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. Young's modulus is longitudinal stress over longitudinal strain: Y = F/AΔ L/L = FLA Δ L, which is II, so A-II.
  2. Compressibility is the reciprocal of bulk modulus: k = 1B = -1Δ P(Δ VV), which is III, so B-III.
  3. Bulk modulus is B = -Δ PΔ V/V = -P(VΔ V), which is IV, so C-IV.
  4. Poisson's ratio is lateral strain over longitudinal strain: σ = Δ d/dΔ L/L = Δ dΔ L(Ld), which is I, so D-I.
  5. A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I is option 4.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
44 highagree
difficultyeasy · 4 steps
stepsSpot FL/A(dL). This is Young's modulus. → Spot -(1/dP)(dV/V). This is compressibility. → Spot -P(V/dV). This is bulk modulus. → Spot (dd/dL)(L/d). This is Poisson's ratio.
confusing options1 of 4 · option 4
Only one option matches A with II. And FL/A(dL) is the one formula here that you can name straight away. So the three options that start with A-IV, A-III and A-I are gone on the first row.
why it is trickyOn paper there are four things to recall. But the options end it after the first one. Once you name Young's modulus, three options go. The slip that would really hurt is swapping compressibility with bulk modulus, because they are reciprocals. That swap is not printed in any option that survives the A row.

ConceptYou have to tell Young's modulus, bulk modulus, compressibility and Poisson's ratio apart from their formulas. Compressibility is simply 1 divided by the bulk modulus.
Where students go wrongReversedreversedthe right thing stated backwards: direction, order or ratiooption 3
Most students pick option 3. Compressibility is 1 divided by the bulk modulus. Many students remember that the two go together but forget which way round. So they read -P(VΔ V) as compressibility. Option 3 is the only code that pairs B with IV. The correct way is the other way round. The 1Δ P form is compressibility. So B goes with III and C goes with IV.

Q3Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterSemiconductor Electronics high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on deciding which ideal diodes are forward biased and therefore conduct, which is diode circuit behaviour taught with the semiconductor diode.
subtopic 1PN Junction Diode Under Forward Bias
subtopic 2PN Junction Diode Under Reverse Bias
why this subtopicThe answer 15/2 A depends on seeing that only the forward-biased branches (4 ohm and 2 ohm) conduct as ideal shorts while the reverse-biased branches (3 ohm, 5 ohm) carry no current, giving R = 4/3 ohm across 10 V.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
The current I in the circuit shown below is: (All diodes are ideal and identical)
  1. 53 A
  2. 59 A
  3. 13 A
  4. 152 A
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
  1. For ideal diode, forward resistance = 0 and reverse biased resistance = ∞
  2. ∴ Circuit can be redrawn as,
  3. I = 102 + 104
  4. = 304 = 152 A

→ the working concludes: option 4

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. The battery's + plate feeds the left rail, so conventional current leaves it upward (as the arrow I shows) and crosses every branch from left to right.
  2. A diode conducts only when its arrowhead points along the current, i.e. to the right: that is true for the 4 Ω branch and the 2 Ω branch.
  3. The diodes in the 3 Ω and 5 Ω branches point left, so they are reverse biased and those branches carry no current.
  4. The two conducting branches are in parallel: Req = 4 × 24 + 2 = 43 Ω.
  5. I = VReq = 104/3 = 304 = 152 A, which is option 4.

stepsCheck each ideal diode. Is it forward biased or reverse biased? → Replace every conducting diode with a plain wire. Replace every reverse biased diode with a break in the circuit. → Simplify the resistors that are left and use Ohm's law to find I.

chapterRotational Motion medium confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on rotational kinematics for a rigid body spinning up at constant angular acceleration, average angular speed x time giving 150 revolutions.
subtopic 1Angular Velocity and Angular Acceleration
why this subtopicThe answer depends on uniformly accelerated angular motion - the revolutions equal the mean angular speed (600+1200)/2 rpm times 10 s, i.e. 150 revolutions.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
The angular speed of a flywheel is increased from 600 rpm to 1200 rpm in 10 s. The number of revolutions completed by the flywheel during this time is:
  1. 900
  2. 600
  3. 150
  4. 300
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)
  1. α = ω2 - ω1Δ t = (1200 - 60010)2π60 = 2π rad/s2
  2. ⇒ Use equation of motion, ω22 = ω12 + 2αθ
  3. ⇒ ω2 = 1200 × 2π60 = 40π
  4. ω1 = 600 × 2π60 = 20π
  5. (40π)2 = (20π)2 + 2 × 2πθ
  6. ⇒ 1200 π2 = 4πθ
  7. ⇒ θ = 300π radian
  8. ⇒ Number of revolution = θ2π = 150

→ the working concludes: option 3

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
  1. Convert both rates to revolutions per second: n1 = 60060 = 10 rev/s and n2 = 120060 = 20 rev/s.
  2. With uniform angular acceleration the mean rate is n = n1 + n22 = 10 + 202 = 15 rev/s.
  3. N = n t = 15 × 10 = 150 revolutions, which is option 3.

READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
A ray of monochromatic light is passing through an equilateral prism (ABC) as shown in the figure. The refracted ray (QR) is parallel to its base (BC) and the angle of incidence (i) is 50°. Then the angle of deviation (δ) is:
  1. 45°

  2. The refracted ray QR running parallel to the base BC is the symmetric passage, i.e. the minimum-deviation configuration, where e = i and r1 = r2 = A/2.
  3. Prism relation: δ = i + e - A = 2i - A.
  4. δ = 2 × 50° - 60° = 40°, which is option 3.

subjectPhysics
chapterCurrent Electricity high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on the metre bridge balance condition being unchanged when the cell and galvanometer are interchanged, so deflection still reverses either side of the same null point.
subtopic 1Meter Bridge
why this subtopicThe answer depends on the metre bridge being a Wheatstone network whose balance condition is unchanged when the cell and galvanometer arms are swapped, so deflections still occur on both sides and vanish at the balance point.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
In a metre bridge experiment (see figure), the positions of the cell, E, and galvanometer, G, are interchanged. We shall observe in the galvanometer:
  1. Only the left-sided deflection
  2. There will be no deflection irrespective of the position of the jockey
  3. Only the right-sided deflection
  4. Both right-sided and left-sided deflection and at balance point, no deflection
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
  1. Position of null point will not change when galvanometer (G) and the cell (E) are interchanged.
  2. There will be no deflection in galvanometer only at balance point.
  3. In an unbalanced meter bridge, if E and G are interchanged mutually, then the deflection in galvanometer may be towards left-side or right-side.

→ the working concludes: option 4

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. A metre bridge is a Wheatstone network: R1 and R2 in the gaps, the two parts of the wire as the other arms, with the cell across one diagonal and the galvanometer across the other.
  2. Balance means the galvanometer diagonal carries no current, i.e. the two junctions are at equal potential; algebraically R1R2 = l100 - l.
  3. This condition is symmetric in the two diagonals, so interchanging the cell and the galvanometer leaves the balance point exactly where it was.
  4. Therefore the galvanometer still deflects one way on one side of the null point and the other way on the other side, with zero deflection at balance: option 4.

So swapping them leaves the balance condition the same. → Turn that into what you actually see as the jockey slides: deflection one way on one side of the balance point, the other way past it, and zero deflection where the condition is met.

Nothing in the circuit makes left different from right, so once you notice that you drop both on sight.

Which of the following statements are correct?

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
A.Inside a conductor, the electrostatic field is zero.
B.Electric field at the surface of a charged conductor does not depend on its surface charge density.
C.The interior of a charged conductor can have no excess charge in the static situation.
D.At the surface of a charged conductor, the electrostatic field must be normal to the surface at every point.
E.The electrostatic potential is zero everywhere inside a charged conductor.

  2. A, C and E only
  3. A, C and D only
  4. C, D and E only
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)
  1. A. Electrostatic field is zero inside a conductor.
  2. B. Electric field at the surface of a charged conductor = σε0ˆn, depends on surface charge density (σ).
  3. C. The interior of a charged conductor cannot have any excess charge in the static situation.
  4. D. At the surface of a charged conductor, the electrostatic field ⊥ surface.
  5. E. The electrostatic potential is constant and can be non-zero everywhere inside a charged conductor.

→ the working concludes: option 3

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
  1. A: in electrostatic equilibrium free charges have redistributed until the net field inside the conducting material is zero. True.
  2. B: just outside a charged conductor →E = σε0ˆn, which depends directly on the local surface charge density. False.
  3. C: by Gauss's law applied to any interior surface, the enclosed charge is zero, so all excess charge resides on the outer surface. True.
  4. D: any tangential component would drive surface charge along the surface, contradicting equilibrium, so the field at the surface must be normal at every point. True.
  5. E: the conductor is an equipotential, so the potential inside equals the surface potential - a constant, but not zero in general (a charged isolated conductor is at a non-zero potential). False.
  6. A, C and D only is option 3.

printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
Consider the following reaction :

2A(g) + B(g) → 2D(g)

Δ U⊖ = -10 kJ mol-1 and Δ S⊖ = -44 JK-1 at 298 K.

Identify the correct option with Δ G⊖ for the reaction and spontaneity of the reaction at 298 K.

(Given : R = 8.31 J mol-1 K-1)
  1. -1.635 kJ mol-1, spontaneous
  2. -0.63568 kJ mol-1, spontaneous
  3. +0.63568 kJ mol-1, non-spontaneous
  4. +1.635 kJ mol-1, non-spontaneous
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)
  1. 2A(g) + B(g) → 2D(g)
  2. Δ U° = -10 kJ/mol
  3. Δ S° = -44 J/K
  4. Δ H° = Δ U° + Δ ng RT
  5. Δ H° = -10 - 1 × 298 × (8.31)1000 = -10 - 2.48 = -12.48 kJ/mol
  6. Δ G° = Δ H° - TΔ S°
  7. = -12.48 - 298 × (-44)1000
  8. = -12.48 + 13.112
  9. = +0.632 kJ/mol
  10. Since Δ G° comes out to be positive, so given process is non-spontaneous.

→ the working concludes: option 3

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
  1. Change in moles of gas: Δ ng = 2 - (2 + 1) = -1.
  2. Δ H⊖ = Δ U⊖ + Δ ng RT = -10000 + (-1)(8.31)(298).
  3. (8.31)(298) = 2476.4 J, so Δ H⊖ = -10000 - 2476.4 = -12476.4 J mol-1.
  4. TΔ S⊖ = 298 × (-44) = -13112 J.
  5. Δ G⊖ = Δ H⊖ - TΔ S⊖ = -12476.4 + 13112 = +635.6 J mol-1 = +0.636 kJ mol-1.
  6. Δ G⊖ > 0, so the reaction is non-spontaneous: option 3.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict

stepsCount the change in the number of gas moles: 2 moles of product against 3 of reactant, so Dn = -1 → Change internal energy into enthalpy: DH = DU + Dn RT = -10000 + (-1)(8.31)(298) = -12476 J → Work out TDS = 298 x (-44) = -13112 J and subtract: DG = DH - TDS = -12476 + 13112 → Change the small leftover back into kJ and read its sign to say whether the reaction is spontaneous

And the options are built as a matched pair with opposite signs, so a sign slip lands exactly on option 2 instead of on nothing.
the catchThe step students skip is turning DU into DH with the Dn RT term. If you skip it you get +3.1 kJ, which matches nothing. But if you get its sign wrong, or the sign of TDS wrong, you land exactly on the printed twin. And the answer is a small leftover from two large terms, so there is no rough size check available.

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · medium
  1. Pick the longest continuous carbon chain; for this skeleton it runs through seven carbons, so the parent is heptane and names based on hexane (options 2 and 4) are wrong.
  2. The two branches on that heptane chain are one ethyl and one methyl, so 'diethyl' names are wrong.
  3. Numbering from either end gives the locant set {3,5}, a tie, so the rule is to give the lowest locant to the substituent cited first alphabetically.
  4. Alphabetically ethyl precedes methyl, so ethyl takes 3 and methyl takes 5, and the substituents are cited in that same alphabetical order.
  5. That gives 3-ethyl-5-methylheptane, option 1; option 3 is the same skeleton written with the locants and alphabetical order both wrong.

stepsFind the longest unbroken chain in the drawing. It is seven carbons, not the six your eye follows first. → Number from both ends and compare the two sets of positions. They tie at 3 and 5. → Break the tie with the rule that the substituent that comes first alphabetically takes the lower number. So ethyl gets 3. → Put the name together with the substituents listed alphabetically.

All four names are C10H22, and options 1, 2 and 3 all describe the same skeleton. Option 2 picks a six-carbon parent instead of the seven-carbon one. Option 3 is the correct chain numbered from the wrong end, which gives the same set of positions, 3 and 5. So the usual lowest-numbers check cannot reject it.
why it is trickyThis is hard not because it is long, but because the deciding rule is never signposted. The lowest-numbers test ties, and only the alphabetical tiebreak separates 3-ethyl-5-methylheptane from 3-methyl-5-ethylheptane. Meanwhile the wrong-parent-chain name sits there as a third live option for anyone who traces the drawn chain straight across instead of hunting for the longest one.
the catchYou need two naming rules, one after the other, and the second one, that the alphabetically first substituent wins a tie, is the one most students never learn. The wrong options are built on one broken rule each, not at random.

  1. Formal charge = Valence electrons (V) - 12 (shared electrons) (S) - (non-bonding electrons) (L)
  2. Formal charge on 2nd oxygen atom = 6 - 12(4) - 4 = 0
  3. Formal charge on 1st oxygen atom = 6 - 12(6) - 2 = +1

  1. Formal charge = (valence electrons) - (lone pair electrons) - 12(bonding electrons), and each oxygen has 6 valence electrons.
  2. Atom 2 is the doubly bonded terminal oxygen with two lone pairs: FC = 6 - 4 - 12(4) = 0.
  3. Atom 1 is the central oxygen with one lone pair and three bonds (one double, one single): FC = 6 - 2 - 12(6) = +1.
  4. Atom 3 is the singly bonded terminal oxygen with three lone pairs: FC = 6 - 6 - 12(2) = -1.
  5. The charges sum to zero, as they must for neutral O3.
  6. Taken in the asked order 2, 1, 3 the answer is 0, +1, -1, which is option 2.

  3. 1 - x    2x

  1. The reaction over hot coke is CO2(g) + C(s) → 2CO(g), and the carbon is a solid so only the gases count in the volumes.

publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
Identify the incorrect statement from the following :
  1. The largest and the smallest species among Mg, Mg2+, Al and Al3+ are Al and Mg2+ respectively.
  2. The IUPAC name of the element with atomic number 107 is Unnilseptium.
  3. The similarity in behaviour of Li with Mg is referred to as 'diagonal relationship'
  4. The oxidation state and covalency of Al in [AlCl(H2O)5]2+ are 3 and 6, respectively.
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)
  1. The largest species is Mg and the smallest one is Al3+ among Mg, Mg2+, Al and Al3+.
  2. Unnilseptium element has atomic number 107
  3. Li and Mg are diagonally related and have similar properties.
  4. The oxidation state and covalency of Al in [AlCl(H2O)5]2+ are +3 and 6 respectively
  5. ∴ Statement A is incorrect

→ the working concludes: option 1

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
  1. Across period 3 the nuclear charge rises while the shell stays the same, so the neutral atom shrinks: Mg > Al.
  2. Both cations have the neon configuration, so the one with the higher nuclear charge is smaller: Mg2+ > Al3+, and both are far smaller than the parent atoms.
  3. The full order is Mg > Al > Mg2+ > Al3+, so the largest is Mg and the smallest is Al3+; statement 1 names Al and Mg2+ and is therefore wrong.
  4. Statement 2 is correct: 107 gives un-nil-sept-ium, Unnilseptium, in the IUPAC systematic naming of elements above 100.
  5. Statement 3 is correct: lithium resembles magnesium, the standard example of a diagonal relationship.
  6. Statement 4 is correct: in [AlCl(H2O)5]2+ aluminium is in the +3 oxidation state and is bonded to six donor atoms, so its covalency is 6.
  7. The incorrect statement is option 1.

Option 2 tempts you if you learned that element 107 is Bohrium. You then call the systematic name wrong, not realising NCERT prints both. Option 4 tempts you because oxidation state and covalency get mixed up all the time, and the overall 2+ charge on the ion invites you to read the oxidation state off the charge. Option 1 tempts you because Al sits to the right of Mg, and you have to apply the across-the-period trend to a mixed set of atoms and cations.

And oxidation state against covalency in a complex ion. Each one needs its own separate check. Three of them have a printed route to being called the odd one out, so crossing out gets you nowhere. Only the Li and Mg line is safe to drop.

READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
Mixture of chloroform and acetone forms a solution with negative deviation from Raoult's law due to :
  1. Increase in escaping tendency of molecules of each component.
  2. Formation of hydrogen bonding between acetone and chloroform
  3. Stronger intermolecular forces between chloroform molecules than those between chloroform and acetone molecules.
  4. Repulsive forces.
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (2)
  1. Acetone and chloroform show negative deviation from Raoult's law due to stronger H-bonding between acetone and chloroform mixture.
  2. Hence, escaping tendency decreases
  3. ∴ Vapour pressure decreases
  4. ∴ Boiling point increases.

→ the working concludes: option 2

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 2 · high
  1. Negative deviation from Raoult's law means the observed vapour pressure is lower than predicted, which happens when the new A-B interaction is stronger than the original A-A and B-B interactions.
  2. The three electronegative chlorines of CHCl3 leave its single hydrogen strongly positive, so it can hydrogen bond to the lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen of acetone.
  3. This extra attraction holds the molecules in the liquid, lowering the escaping tendency and so the vapour pressure of both components, which is exactly negative deviation.
  4. That is option 2; option 1 describes positive deviation, and options 3 and 4 describe weaker A-B interaction, which would also give positive deviation.

Option 3 is the only wrong option with any pull. It also compares intermolecular forces, so it is the right kind of explanation. But it has the comparison the wrong way round, like with like stronger than unlike, and that is the condition for positive deviation. Options 1 and 4, rising escaping tendency and repulsive forces, are positive-deviation language. The word 'negative' in the question kills both.

    Which of the following statements are correct with respect to DNA separation, isolation and visualization?

    Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
    A.The cutting of DNA is done by molecular scissors.

    D.The separated DNA fragments, when stained with ethidium bromide, can be seen in visible light.
    1. B and D only
    2. A and B only
    3. B and C only
    4. A and D only
    The publisher's solutionprinted answer (2)
    1. The cutting of DNA is possible by the use of restriction enzymes that results in the fragments of DNA. These fragments of DNA can be separated by a technique known as gel electrophoresis.
    2. The DNA fragments separate (resolve) according to their size through sieving effect provided by the agarose gel.
    3. The separated DNA fragments can be visualised only after staining the DNA with a compound known as ethidium bromide followed by exposure to UV radiation.

    → the working concludes: option 2

    printed solution, as in the booklet
    Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 2 · high
    1. A is correct: NCERT Class 12, Ch. 11 (Biotechnology: Principles and Processes) calls restriction endonucleases molecular scissors, which cut the DNA.

    3. C is incorrect: NCERT states the separated DNA fragments can be visualised only after staining the DNA with a compound known as ethidium bromide - they are not visible unstained.
    4. D is incorrect: after ethidium bromide staining, the bright orange-coloured DNA bands are seen on exposure to UV radiation, not in visible light.

    2. The mother's gametes are IA and i, each with probability 12; the father's are IB and i, each with probability 12.

    2. A neural signal reaching neuromuscular junction releases a neurotransmitter (Acetylcholine) which generates an action potential in the sarcolemma.     Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
    1. NCERT Class 12, Ch. 13 (Organisms and Populations) tabulates interspecific interactions by the sign of the effect on each species.
    2. B is correct: mutualism is (+,+), both species benefit.
    3. D is correct: parasitism is (+,-), one species benefits and the other is harmed.
    4. E is correct: amensalism is (-,0), one species is harmed and the other is unaffected.
    5. A is incorrect because it lumps commensalism with parasitism; commensalism is (+,0), so the second species is not harmed.
    6. C is incorrect for the same reason: in commensalism only one species benefits, the other is neither harmed nor benefited.
    7. So B, D and E only, option 3.
